1:
Why the errand fell to a young man rather than to the prophet himself is answered in full by Henry. Elisha was old, unfit for the journey, and too well known to go and return unobserved; the service carried danger a younger life might better run; and since anointing a king was an honour, he would not engross it but gave one of the sons of the prophets a share. On who the messenger was, three voices follow one tradition: Gill and Clarke report that the Jews make him Jonah the son of Amittai, and Ellicott credits Rashi with it. Clarke nonetheless renders the phrase at the next verse as the servant of the prophet, the attendant Elisha then had in Gehazi's place, and Ellicott agrees it means Elisha's minister, noting that some manuscripts and versions drop the second occurrence.

Henry observes that Solomon was anointed with oil out of the tabernacle, no longer to be had, and holds oil from a prophet's hand equivalent to oil out of God's house; he adds that anointing was probably not constant practice but was used when a succession was disturbed or the crown passed to a new family. On the order to flee the readings divide three ways. Keil and Delitzsch reject the view they ascribe to Theodoret, that it guarded the messenger against Ahab's secret adherents, preferring Schmidt's, that it prevented further discussion; Ellicott has it avoid questioning and give the act greater force. Henry reads the privacy itself as a test: with no witness to attest the commission, Jehu's being suddenly animated for the work was proof enough, the thing signified being the best evidence of the sign.

On the title the voices converge, then one turns on a critic. Clarke takes king over the people of the Lord to mean that Jehu was to rule them by God's law and so restore the pure worship. Henry presses both halves: made king by the God of Israel, from whom his power came and to whom he was accountable, and over the Israel of God, a people still called the Lord's though corrupted, since God had not yet given them a bill of divorce, so that they were God's freemen and not Jehu's vassals. Ellicott puts it as sovereign right, Jehovah being Israel's true king and free to appoint his earthly representative. Whether the anointing had happened once already divides them. Henry rejects the supposition that Elijah had done it privately beforehand, as Samuel did for David, because then Hazael must have been anointed privately too. Ellicott treats the act as Elijah's commission discharged by his successor, and answers Reuss, who held this narrative substituted for something another document told of Elijah, that the conjecture is pure, and, when Reuss went on to make Elisha a revolutionary whose name the new dynasty used for legitimacy, that this is being considerably wiser than our only authorities.

The ground of the sentence is where Henry and Wesley speak almost with one voice. Both set the idolatry aside, bad as it was, because it is not what is mentioned, and fix the controversy on persecution: nothing so fills the measure of a prince's iniquity, or brings a surer and sorer ruin, as the blood of the prophets. Clarke grounds the justice in the standing law that whoever sheds man's blood shall have his own shed, the murders having forfeited their lives. Gill meets the objection from loyalty, Jehu being Ahab's captain and his son's, with the answer that an order from the King of kings vindicated what would otherwise be treason. Ellicott allows as probable, though unattested elsewhere, that Jezebel had persecuted to the death those who clung to the exclusive worship of Jehovah; Keil and Delitzsch observe that the threat only repeats what the earlier book pronounced.
11:
The captains' word for the messenger is where most of the comment gathers. Henry hears pure contempt, with the unspoken question whether prophets are company for captains, and explains the name by the life: the man would not run with them to an excess of riot but lived in self-denial, and those who have no religion commonly take the religious for mad. He instances the charges that our Saviour was beside himself and that much learning had made Paul mad. Wesley follows the same track and the same instances, adding that they knew him for a prophet by his habit, gestures and manner of speech. Clarke turns it into a rebuke of the officers, asking whether a holy man of God was reputed a madman by a club of irreligious soldiers, since those who scoff at holy men pretend in vain to fight for religion. Ellicott offers a softer alternative, that the word may be ridicule for one inspired, and puts their alarm first: they dreaded sinister news and were struck by his wild bearing and haste.

Jehu's answer is read three ways. Henry takes it as a reproof turned back on them: they knew the man for a prophet and should not call him mad, or else his errand was guessable, to tell Jehu of his faults. Clarke has Jehu agreeing with their contempt as a way of putting them off, unwilling to say what had been done lest it breed jealousy and envy. Ellicott puts the emphasis on the pronoun and has Jehu probing them, implying they had sent the man and planned it, or more probably asking why they question him when they must have divined the answer. On the second noun the versions pull apart, and Ellicott lines them up: the Greek makes it babble, the Targum a story, the Vulgate simply what he said, the Arabic his news.

Their refusal takes a different force in each voice. Gill reconstructs their reasoning: the messenger's haste, the privacy, Jehu's thoughtful countenance and his trifling reply together convinced them something had passed. Keil and Delitzsch render the retort flatly as a denial that he spoke truth; Clarke reports the Chaldee as thou liest,. Ellicott thinks the English too strong and would have the one word mean trickery, that Jehu was pretending and evading, with a coaxing request following it. He draws the consequence that matters: whether or not they had already guessed the errand, their manner satisfied Jehu that he could safely trust them.

What the garments were and where they were laid divides the voices twice over. Keil and Delitzsch take them for the single large cloth wrapped about the body, spread in place of carpets upon the steps to serve as a throne; Gill denies they were wearing apparel at all and makes them carpets or tapestry, laid so Jehu might sit raised and conspicuous. Clarke compares the multitudes who owned Jesus as Messiah and king, and reads the ceremony as a confession: putting their garments under his feet, they put everything under his authority and owned themselves his servants. The place is harder. Gill reports the Targum's reading of a stone engraved with the twelve hours, and Clarke builds on it, holding with the rabbins that this was the public sun-dial, built in steps so each threw the shadow of an hour, and very probably the same dial on which the sign was afterwards given to Ahaz. Keil and Delitzsch cut against all of it: the early translators merely guessed, and the phrase can hardly mean anything but Kimchi's upon the bare steps themselves, the Arabic-based rendering of Lud. de Dieu having no analogy in Hebrew. Henry adds the political reading, that Jehu did nothing without the captains' consent, since those who would rise fast and stand firm take their friends along with them.
14:
Gill states the plot plainly: Jehu and the captains with him entered a confederacy to depose Joram and set up Jehu in his place. The condition Jehu attaches to it is handled as a matter of idiom. Keil and Delitzsch render the clause as a question of their wish, and Ellicott gives the Hebrew literally as if it be your soul, notes the manuscripts that read if it be with your soul, and judges that the Latin paraphrases it correctly as if it please you. The order itself Ellicott also takes literally, that not a fugitive should go forth. Keil and Delitzsch add a small textual observation on the written form of the infinitive in the command, which the margin would correct and which they would leave standing, since syncope of that kind has many parallels.

Out of that order three voices draw the same military conclusion, and it settles a disputed point. Ellicott argues from the command that Ramoth must have been in the hands of the Israelite army, since the prohibition makes no sense if they were themselves besieging the place, which is what Josephus relates. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same result from the other direction, taking the verb used of Joram to mean that he had been holding the city against the attacks of Hazael, not laying siege to it, and concluding that the Israelites were in possession and defending it. Clarke fills in the campaign: the confederate armies appear to have taken the city, and were then obliged to watch their conquest, seeing that Hazael meant to retake it if he could. The same verses account for Joram's absence, Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch both having him wounded in the attack on Ramoth and gone down to Jezreel to be cured.

On the ride itself the voices part over what the chariot signified. Gill sees state in it, Jehu riding in great pomp and majesty as a king. Henry sees nothing but speed: the distance from Ramoth-gilead to Jezreel was more than one day's march, with the Jordan to be crossed about midway, and he supposes Jehu to have marched with all possible expedition and to have taken the utmost precaution that the news should not outrun him. Keil and Delitzsch put the same thing in a phrase, that he drove to Jezreel without delay. All three agree on what waited at the end of it, Joram lying there under his wounds, with Ahaziah come down on a visit to him.
17:
The watchman is explained first as an institution. Gill gives him his ordinary duty of spying an enemy far off and giving notice, and adds that he was the more needful now because the king was in the town. Clarke widens it into a system: such watchmen were posted on high ground within hearing of one another and served as a kind of telegraph for passing intelligence through the whole country, though in some cases, as here, the news went on by a horseman to the next stage; with the armies away at Ramoth they would have been doubly watchful. Ellicott fixes the place, the tower being attached to the palace and the palace perhaps near the eastern wall, and takes the word for what the watchman saw to mean an overflow, used elsewhere of a multitude of waters, of camels and of horses, from which he infers that Jehu had a considerable force with him. Keil and Delitzsch note only that the form of the word is a rarer one. Ellicott adds that the king's order was given not to the watchman but to a courtier, the narrative being very concise.

What the king's question meant is disputed. Gill takes it broadly, as asking whether all was well with the army or there was a disturbance in the kingdom, and whether the riders came as friends or enemies. Ellicott holds that the English hardly represents the force of it and that Joram was not yet apprehensive at all: he was expecting news from Ramoth, and the words mean no more than what is the news. Against Thenius, who made it a demand whether they came with friendly or hostile intention, he asks whether a king who suspected that would have sent a single horseman to find out. The answer returned is read the same way by both of the voices that gloss it. Keil and Delitzsch render it as a refusal to let the messenger trouble himself about peace, with the following words an order to fall in behind; Ellicott calls it a rough evasion, Jehu being conscious of his strength and able to despise a royal message, the messenger not daring to disobey, and the object plainly to keep any alarm from reaching Jezreel. On the second rider Ellicott prefers the reading that repeats the question to the received text that makes it a greeting, and observes that Joram, still unsuspicious, might well have supposed some accident had detained the first.

The driving is the crux of the passage, and the testimony runs both ways. Clarke makes it character: Jehu was a bold, daring, prompt and precipitate general whose manner was established by his campaigns and had become almost proverbial. Keil and Delitzsch render the watchman's words as driving like a madman, and gloss the state as headlong haste. Ellicott ties the word to the very one the captains had used of the prophet, and pictures the chariot swaying unsteadily as Jehu drove madly on. Then he reports the contrary tradition without adopting it: the Targum explains the word in exactly the opposite sense, as quietly, and Josephus has Jehu driving rather slowly and in orderly fashion, which Ellicott suspects came of confusing the word for madness with a similar one meaning a slow mournful song. He notes too that Jehu is called son of Nimshi here where the fuller descent would be expected, and that two of the versions do the same earlier in the chapter.
21:
That the kings went out unguarded is taken by two voices as proof they suspected nothing. Clarke says they had no notion of what had been done at Ramoth-gilead, or would never have ventured their persons so; Ellicott reasons the same way from their leaving the walls without an escort, and supplies the curiosity that drew them: why the messengers had not returned, and why the commander-in-chief had quitted the seat of war. Where they met him is given weight. Ellicott notes that Naboth's vineyard by now formed part of the pleasure-grounds of the palace, and Wesley says the sight of that ground alone was enough to make Jehu triumph and Joram tremble, providence sometimes ordering the circumstances of an event so that the punishment answers the sin as face answers face in a glass.

The charge Jehu returns divides the voices three ways. Clarke takes the words in their common and most obvious sense, holding there is much reason to think Jezebel patronised a genuinely impure religion, and adding the shrewd observation that Jehu would hardly have been objecting to the calf-worship, to which he was himself favourably disposed. Ellicott takes them in the spiritual sense of idolatries, and renders the question as asking what peace there can be while those things continue. Wesley allows both at once: the literal, because spiritual whoredom is often punished with corporal, and the spiritual, because departing from God is whoredom and sorcery bewitches the mind and is a plain covenant with the devil. On the sorceries Ellicott supplies the background, spells and charms being common among Semitic idolaters and forbidden in the Law, with Babylonia the home of the whole pseudo-science. Wesley answers why the mother's sins and not the son's: hers were the more notorious, and the principal cause of the judgment Jehu came to execute.

The flight and the shot are closely construed. Gill has Joram take the reins himself or signal the charioteer; Ellicott renders it as turning the horses round. Keil and Delitzsch make the cry mean that they are deceived, in fact betrayed, and Clarke notes this was Joram's first intimation of it. On the bow the two grammatical voices come into open conflict. Clarke endorses the marginal reading, that Jehu filled his hand with a bow, allowing no other sense than that he took it up, set his arrow and let fly; Keil and Delitzsch gloss the idiom as seizing the bow. Ellicott names that explanation and rejects it: the margin is not quite accurate, the phrase means Jehu had meanwhile set an arrow on the bow ready to shoot, and to fill a bow is to stretch it. On the wound they agree, the arrow entering obliquely between the shoulders as Joram fled and coming out at the heart. Wesley reduces the whole to one line, that it was one of God's arrows, ordained against the persecutor.

The oracle Jehu recalls comes last. Gill is careful that Bidkar was Jehu's captain now, though he had served Joram and Ahab before; Ellicott, taking the rank as adjutant, reports the form of the name meaning son of stabbing, a fit name for Jehu's squire. How the two men had ridden behind Ahab is less certain. Keil and Delitzsch prefer riding in pairs, with most commentators, while allowing the reading of Kimchi and Bochart that makes them two men in one chariot; Ellicott agrees on riding side by side, and lists the Targum, the Latin and Kimchi for the single chariot. Clarke takes up the blood of Naboth's sons, which the earlier account does not mention: since Ahab and Jezebel wanted the vineyard outright and for ever, they would hardly leave posterity who might reclaim the inheritance, and the conviction for treason was framed to involve the whole family in the ruin.
27:
The pursuit is reconstructed mostly by Ellicott. The garden house he takes as a direction rather than a destination, probably an arbour or drinking pavilion by the gates of the palace gardens, of which Naboth's ground formed part, Ahaziah's object being to get clear of the royal park as fast as he could. The order to shoot he thinks the Hebrew renders far more fitly to the excitement of the moment than the English does, Jehu simply ejaculating that this one too should be shot in his chariot. Something has then dropped out of the text: the Syriac supplies that they slew him in his chariot, but Ellicott prefers the Greek as involving the least change and being the more graphic, Jehu himself shooting his second victim after a hot pursuit at the ascent of Gur, where a chariot would have to slacken. Keil and Delitzsch read the wound as mortal but not immediately fatal, inflicted at the height of Gur near Jibleam, so that Ahaziah died as he fled on to Megiddo, and they too supply the missing clause as lost by a copyist. On the places Ellicott notes that the ascent of Gur occurs nowhere else, that Ibleam lay between Jezreel and Megiddo, and that Megiddo appears in the cuneiform inscriptions.

How this account squares with the other is the real question in these verses, and four answers are on the table. Clarke sets out the difficulty plainly, that in the later history Jehu sought Ahaziah, who was caught hiding in Samaria, brought to Jehu, killed and buried, which is very different from what stands here; and he gives the harmony at length from Lightfoot. On that reading Ahaziah saw Joram killed in the field of Jezreel and fled to hide in Samaria, while Jehu went on to Jezreel and to Jezebel, sent for the heads of Ahab's children, and marched to Samaria, where the search found Ahaziah and he was carried off towards Gur by Ibleam and smitten there, his charioteer driving on to Megiddo before he died; Kings is short, and Chronicles shows the order. Wesley harmonises too and holds that Chronicles was in great part written to supply what Kings omits, but his sequence runs the other way, Megiddo first, then Samaria, the capture, the sentence from Jehu, and death at Megiddo. Ellicott will have none of it. The definite assignment of places here he counts a mark of greater trustworthiness, the attempt of Rashi, whom he says Keil follows, to combine the two narratives is revolting to common sense, and it would be better to assume that one text or the other is corrupt.

The burial and the date are quieter. Gill has the body carried to Jerusalem by Jehu's leave, granted because Ahaziah was Jehoshaphat's grandson and so of a line that had worshipped God sincerely; Ellicott renders the verb as making him ride, notes that three versions supply the words the Hebrew almost demands, and takes the tomb to be one the king had prepared in his own lifetime after the custom of antiquity. The regnal year then divides them. Gill reckons the eleventh and the twelfth as the close of one and the beginning of the other, or else sees a co-regency, the son beginning with his father in the eleventh and alone in the twelfth; Clarke says the same, that he reigned first as viceroy during his father's sickness and alone from the twelfth. Ellicott sees no difficulty worth harmonising: the synchronisms between the two kingdoms rest on no exact records, different computations could make the same year either, and the verse may be a parenthesis and perhaps not original.
30:
Henry reads the queen's conduct as three refusals. Gill notes that the news reaching her included what Jehu had done to Joram, killed for her own whoredoms and flung into Naboth's ground; and instead of hiding as one afraid of vengeance she exposed herself, scorned to flee and mocked at fear, which is how a heart hardened against God braves it out to the last. Instead of humbling herself or going into mourning for her son she painted and dressed, meaning to look as great as she thought herself and so to put Jehu out of countenance, when the call was to baldness and sackcloth; there is no surer presage of ruin, Henry says, than an unhumbled heart under humbling providences. Instead of trembling before the instrument of vengeance she tried to make him tremble, taking no notice of the hand gone out against her family and flying in the face of the sword in that hand, and pleasing herself that his work would end in his own ruin; it is no new thing that those doing God's work should be reckoned out of the way of peace.

The painting itself is described four times over, and the reason for it three ways. Keil and Delitzsch explain the pigment as antimony ore pounded to a powder with a metallic brilliance, laid on brows and lashes dry or worked with oil and applied with a pencil no thicker than a goose-quill. Ellicott makes it antimony and zinc, the dark border throwing the eye into relief. Clarke, who credits the Targum with reading it as staining the eyes, gathers the practice from everywhere: a traveller in Persia on the languishing black eye counted perfect beauty there, the Roman evidence of Pliny and Juvenal, and Cyprian's rebuke that one should anoint the eyes not with the devil's antimony but with the eye-salve of Christ. On why she did it the voices differ. Henry has her hoping to daunt Jehu. Clarke passes on Jarchi's view that she meant to disarm him and induce him to take her to wife, while Ellicott says simply that she put on her royal apparel to die a queen.

What she then said is the most disputed sentence in the chapter. Henry and Wesley take it as a threat backed by a precedent, Wesley reducing it to a reminder that her brother traitor had very short enjoyment of the benefit of his treason. Clarke reports two quite different senses: Jarchi paraphrased it as telling Jehu that killing his master was nothing new and meant to conciliate rather than provoke, while most of the versions make it an ironical salutation, health to the slayer of his master. Ellicott renders it as a mocking inquiry after the health of this second Zimri, his master's murderer, and offers two accounts of the opening words: Thenius's demand whether it was to be peace or war, or, as Ellicott thinks likelier, Jezebel repeating in defiance the question her son had three times put to Jehu, as a hint that she was now the sovereign to whom he owed an account. Keil and Delitzsch say only that Jehu did not deign to answer her.

Henry alone tests the analogy and finds it false. Had the cases been parallel the precedent would have been fairly cited, judgments on those who went before being meant to warn us off their steps; but Zimri had no warrant and was moved only by his own ambition and cruelty, where Jehu had been anointed by one of the sons of the prophets and acted by order from heaven. He also sets the scene in a longer frame: Jezebel had introduced Baal, killed the prophets, contrived Naboth's murder and stirred up first her husband and then her sons, so that her fall after three reigns stands as a type of the ruin of idolaters and persecutors.
32:
Jehu's call for allies is read as a reckoning rather than a risk. Gill has him look up on hearing her words, and reads the order that follows as throwing her from the window to the ground. Ellicott denies, against Thenius, that it implies Jezebel had prepared resistance: Jehu knew the queen was thoroughly hated by her own household, and the eunuchs who a moment before had crouched before her in servile dread would be glad both to curry favour with the regicide and to pay off their malice on their former tyrant. Keil and Delitzsch pass over her words as unworthy of an answer and have the chamberlains look out of the side windows and throw the queen down at Jehu's command. How she was then trampled divides the voices. All the versions, Ellicott notes, make the horses tread her, and Thenius supposed they were maddened by the blood spirting over them; Ellicott himself takes the singular verb as meaning that Jehu drove over the fallen body, and says Ewald goes beyond the text in having him spurn her with his own feet. Clarke simply recoils: she was already half dashed to pieces by the fall, and the brutal Jehu trampled the mangled body under his horses' feet.

The meal that follows is given a motive. Ellicott has Jehu take possession of the palace he had emptied, and observes that savage warrior as he was he forgot the victim of his violence until his appetite was satisfied, after which he could remember that even Jezebel was of royal rank; a touch of remorse, Ellicott thinks, may perhaps be discerned in the order for her burial. Wesley reads the order as forgetfulness of a different kind, Jehu having let slip the charge given him at the anointing that dogs should eat her. On the title Jehu gives her the two voices supply opposite kinds of information. Clarke lays out the lineage in full: daughter of the king of Tyre, wife of one king of Israel, mother of another, mother-in-law to a king of Judah and grandmother of the next. Wesley attends instead to what Jehu does not say, that he called her a king's daughter and not a king's wife, lest he should seem to show any respect to the house of Ahab, which God had devoted to destruction. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the epithet as meaning the woman smitten by God's curse, and Ellicott refers it to the curse Elijah had pronounced.

What the dogs left is reported plainly and then speculated upon. Keil and Delitzsch have nothing found but the skull, the feet and the hollow hands, the rest eaten and dragged away. Clarke passes on the rabbinical explanation of Jarchi and Kimchi, that those parts were spared because in her festal dances she had danced like a dog on hands and feet with her head moving wantonly, and declines to inquire what else they meant by it; he closes on how literally the prediction was fulfilled, and how dearly Jezebel and Ahab paid for Naboth's murder. On the closing oracle Ellicott contradicts his fellow grammarian twice over. Keil and Delitzsch hold the last verse to be a continuation of Elijah's prophecy as quoted by Jehu rather than a remark of the historian, which they ascribe to Luther, but freely expanded by Jehu since it is nowhere given in those words; Ellicott answers that the continuation is probably original and not a free expansion, and on the word for the ground he holds that the earlier book's wall is simply an error from a lost final letter rather than a genuine variant. His own reading is that the remains would no longer be recognisable as Jezebel at all.
